seoTitle: Tachycardia Algorithm: SVT, AFib with RVR, VT and Torsades
metaDescription: Palpitations and tachycardia for EM and IM rotations: cardioversion, modified Valsalva, adenosine, AF rate control, CHA2DS2-VASc, WPW, VT and torsades.
h1: Palpitations and arrhythmia in the ED: the tachycardia algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM or IM rotation with a racing heart on the monitor and a resident about to ask what is next: unstable or not, the 12-lead, SVT from Valsalva to adenosine, AF rate control and anticoagulation, pre-excited AF, wide-complex tachycardia, torsades, hyperkalemia, and what you will be pimped on.

shortAnswer.text: A tachyarrhythmia causing hypotension, confusion, chest pain or heart failure gets synchronized cardioversion now, sedated if awake. A stable patient gets a 12-lead first, before any drug.

shortAnswer.lead: Regular and narrow: Valsalva, then adenosine.
shortAnswer.text: Modified Valsalva first (strain, then lie flat with the legs raised); then adenosine 6 mg rapid push with a flush, 12 mg if no conversion in 1 to 2 minutes.

IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes, verapamil 5 to 10 mg, or an IV beta blocker, never a calcium channel blocker and a beta blocker within hours of each other, and no calcium channel blocker with hypotension or a reduced EF; cardioversion if drugs fail.

shortAnswer.lead: AF: find the driver, then check the EF.
shortAnswer.text: Sepsis, bleeding or PE is treated first, without aggressive rate control. EF over 40%: IV diltiazem or a beta blocker. EF 40% or less: a beta blocker or digoxin, no IV diltiazem or verapamil.

Clear onset under 48 hours, or 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation: early cardioversion is an option. Over 48 hours or unknown: rate control, then 3 weeks of anticoagulation or imaging first (ESC draws the line at 24 hours). Either way, anticoagulation continues at least 4 weeks after.
CHA2DS2-VASc 2 or more in a man, 3 or more in a woman: a DOAC unless there is moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. Aspirin is not an alternative.

shortAnswer.lead: Fast, broad, irregular: no AV nodal blocker.
shortAnswer.text: Stable pre-excited AF gets procainamide or ibutilide, unstable a shock; adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, beta blockers, digoxin and amiodarone can precipitate VF.

shortAnswer.lead: Wide and regular: treat as VT. Twisting: magnesium.
shortAnswer.text: Procainamide, amiodarone or synchronized cardioversion, no verapamil or diltiazem. Torsades: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV whatever the level, and potassium to 4.5 to 5.

sections.heading: What do you do first for palpitations or a tachycardia on the monitor?
sections.intro: Monitor, vitals and a 12-lead during the tachycardia, checking for shock, confusion, chest pain or heart failure. Instability from the rhythm means a shock now; a hyperkalemia pattern on the ECG means IV calcium now.

sections.heading: SVT, AF, flutter, VT or sinus: how do you read the rhythm?
sections.intro: The pulse and vitals sort stable from unstable; the 12-lead then names the branch: regular narrow, AF or flutter, pre-excited AF, regular wide, torsades, a hyperkalemia pattern, sinus, or normal.

sections.heading: How do you treat SVT, AF with RVR, VT and torsades?
sections.intro: Valsalva, adenosine, then a nodal blocker for regular narrow SVT; rate control by the EF and cardioversion by the clock for AF; no nodal blocker in pre-excited AF; VT treatment for a wide regular rhythm of unclear mechanism; magnesium for torsades.

sections.heading: Sinus tachycardia, new AF or a normal ECG: what do you look for?
sections.intro: Sinus tachycardia is a response, so find its cause. New AF: a driver, the EF and thyroid function. A normal ECG between episodes: red flags, then ambulatory monitoring matched to how often it happens.

sections.heading: Who needs anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation?
sections.intro: Score CHA2DS2-VASc whatever the rhythm does next: 2 or more in a man or 3 or more in a woman means anticoagulation; ESC 2024's CHA2DS2-VA drops sex.

sections.heading: Where does each arrhythmia end up?
sections.intro: Converted SVT goes home with cardiology follow-up; AF leaves with a rate plan and a stroke-risk decision; pre-excited AF goes on to ablation; VT is admitted to find the cause.

items.text: A 12-lead recorded during the tachycardia, before any drug.
Stable: no hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, acute heart failure or shock.
Regular and narrow, QRS under 120 ms; not irregular, not wide with pre-excitation.
No bronchospasm, and no second- or third-degree AV block or sinus node disease without a working pacemaker.
Caffeine or theophylline may need a larger dose; dipyridamole means a smaller one.
Rapid push over 1 to 2 seconds as close to the patient as possible, a rapid saline flush, and the ECG recording.

rounds.present: Lead with the rhythm and stability, then the driver, the EF, the clock and the score. For example: 58-year-old man with hypertension and palpitations that began abruptly 18 hours ago; stable, BP 142/88, HR 134. The 12-lead shows atrial fibrillation at 134, narrow QRS, no pre-excitation. No driver: no fever, bleeding, breathlessness or chest pain; echo EF 60% with no valve disease; TSH, hemoglobin and electrolytes normal. The onset is clear and under 48 hours, so early cardioversion is an option: rate control with IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes, or synchronized cardioversion under sedation at 150 to 200 J, with anticoagulation started before and continued at least 4 weeks after. CHA2DS2-VASc 1 for hypertension: long-term anticoagulation is reasonable and decided with him.

pimp.q: Why no adenosine in a fast, broad, irregular rhythm?
pimp.a: If it is pre-excited AF, the accessory pathway, not the AV node, carries the rate, and adenosine and the other AV nodal blockers can precipitate VF or hemodynamic collapse.

pimp.q: Why does adenosine need a rapid push and a flush?
pimp.a: It works only as a rapid bolus, given over 1 to 2 seconds as close to the patient as possible and chased with a rapid saline flush.

pimp.q: What is the modified Valsalva, and how well does it work?
pimp.a: A semi-recumbent strain for about 15 seconds, blowing into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger, then straight to supine with the legs raised. It converted 43% against 17% for the standard strain.

pimp.q: Why no diltiazem in AF with an EF of 30%?
pimp.a: IV diltiazem and verapamil are Class 3: Harm with moderate or severe LV systolic dysfunction. Beta blockers and/or digoxin control the rate there, with IV amiodarone if they fail or cannot be used.

pimp.q: When can AF be cardioverted without 3 weeks of anticoagulation first?
pimp.a: With a clear onset under 48 hours in the US guideline and CAEP, under 24 hours in ESC 2024. The US rule still continues anticoagulation at least 4 weeks after the cardioversion.

pimp.q: Torsades with a normal magnesium. Still give it?
pimp.a: Yes: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV whatever the serum level, repeated if the runs persist, with the offending drug stopped and potassium replaced to 4.5 to 5 mmol/L.

traps.text: Adenosine before the 12-lead in a stable patient. Record the rhythm first.
Diltiazem, adenosine or amiodarone for pre-excited AF. Procainamide or ibutilide, or a shock.
Verapamil for a wide-complex tachycardia called SVT with aberrancy. Treat it as VT.
Rate-controlling AF that sepsis or bleeding is driving. Treat the cause; aggressive rate control is avoided.
Cardioverting stable AF of unknown onset today. Three weeks of anticoagulation or imaging first.
Aspirin instead of anticoagulation, or stopping anticoagulation because sinus rhythm came back. The score decides.
Procainamide or amiodarone for torsades. Magnesium; procainamide is contraindicated and amiodarone prolongs the QT.
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate first for hyperkalemia with ECG changes. IV calcium first.

faq.q: What is the adenosine dose for SVT?
faq.a: 6 mg as a rapid IV bolus over 1 to 2 seconds, as close to the patient as possible, chased with a rapid saline flush. If there is no conversion within 1 to 2 minutes, 12 mg, which the US label allows once more (ESC adds 18 mg). Try a modified Valsalva first, and avoid adenosine with bronchospasm or second- or third-degree AV block.

faq.q: How do you rate control AF with RVR?
faq.a: First look for a driver such as sepsis, bleeding or PE, and treat that instead. With an EF over 40%: IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes (0.35 mg/kg after 15 minutes) or IV metoprolol 2.5 to 5 mg, up to 3 doses. With an EF of 40% or less: a beta blocker or digoxin, never IV diltiazem or verapamil. Aim for a resting rate under 100 to 110.

faq.q: When can you cardiovert atrial fibrillation?
faq.a: At once when it is causing instability. Otherwise when the onset is clearly under 48 hours (24 in ESC 2024) or after 3 weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation; if neither, imaging to exclude intracardiac thrombus first. Anticoagulation continues at least 4 weeks afterward, then by stroke risk. Electrical cardioversion for AF starts at 150 to 200 J.

faq.q: What is the CHA2DS2-VASc cutoff for anticoagulation?
faq.a: 2 or more in a man or 3 or more in a woman: anticoagulate, with a DOAC over warfarin unless there is moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve. 1 in a man or 2 in a woman: reasonable. ESC 2024 uses CHA2DS2-VA without sex: recommended at 2 or more, considered at 1. Aspirin is not an alternative, and flutter is scored the same way.

faq.q: How do you treat a stable wide-complex tachycardia?
faq.a: As VT when the mechanism is not certain: IV procainamide or IV amiodarone (150 mg over 10 minutes, then an infusion), or synchronized cardioversion under sedation, which ESC makes first-line when sedation is safe; US exam answers usually pick a drug first. Never verapamil or diltiazem. Adenosine only if SVT is likely and the resting ECG shows no pre-excitation.

faq.q: What is the first treatment for hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
faq.a: IV calcium, which improves the ECG within about 3 minutes but does not lower the potassium: calcium gluconate 1 g in the US consensus, 6.8 mmol in the UK guideline, repeated if there is no effect in 5 to 10 minutes. Then insulin with glucose and nebulized albuterol, glucose checks for up to 12 hours, and removal, by dialysis in a hemodialysis patient.
